items.title: Rivals in Israel Election Strike Tone of Triumph, but Outcome Is Far From Clear
items.summary: Addressing supporters after midnight, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, who leads a bloc of opposition parties, both expressed confidence that they will lead Israel’s next government. Vote counting could take days.
items.full_text: Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war. The exit polls, if accurate, suggest that neither Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc nor the one led by Mr. Eisenkot , a former military chief whose son was killed in the Gaza war, will be able to form a government without relying on two Arab parties that were projected to win as many as 17 or 18 seats in Parliament. Mr. Netanyahu effectively ruled out including them in a governing coalition, and Mr. Eisenkot and his partners have balked at the idea, too. One option analysts are already weighing is whether Mr. Netanyahu, who has led the most far-right government in Israeli history, could join with Mr. Eisenkot or others in the opposition to form a unity government. But a unity government would face major obstacles, given how deeply Mr. Eisenkot’s voters despise Mr. Netanyahu, and because the two would have to agree on which of them would serve as prime minister. Mr. Netanyahu is unlikely to give up control, while Mr. Eisenkot has called the prime minister unfit to lead Israel. Much remained unclear early Wednesday morning in Israel. Making matters even murkier, Israel’s exit polls have a spotty history of accuracy, particularly in tight races. Mr. Eisenkot appeared onstage past midnight at his post-election party and attempted to strike a tone of triumph — as well as defiance toward Mr. Netanyahu. “Tonight we got the answer: The public wants change,” he said. Mr. Netanyahu addressed his supporters a few hours later, invoking his relationship with President Trump and repeating his pre-election talking points about removing the threat of Iran. He sounded triumphant, saying it was clear that Likud had emerged as the largest party in Israel and mocking months of pre-election polls that showed his party trailing behind that of Mr. Eisenkot. “We must form a strong right-wing government,” he declared. In the coming days, after official vote totals are released and parliamentary seats are allocated to parties, Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will invite the party leader he thinks has the best chance to assemble a governing coalition. Such a coalition would usually have to be made up of at least 61 lawmakers, though Mr. Eisenkot has floated the idea of forming a minority government. One factor not reflected in exit polls are the hundreds of thousands of votes cast by Israelis at special polling stations, including at military bases, hospitals, prisons and embassies. In the previous election, those votes tended to favor the coalition of Mr. Netanyahu and his allies. Here’s what else to know: Arab parties: The exit polls pointed to at least one surprise in projecting that two Arab parties would win as many as 17 or 18 seats in the 120-seat Parliament. That would be their strongest showing ever, and potentially give them an important role in forming the next government. Read more › War fears: Amid reports that Mr. Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Mr. Eisenkot warned him in his speech to supporters not to abuse his power as caretaker prime minister to influence the process of forming a new government. “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” he said. Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, told a television interviewer that the turnout showed that Arab voters, who make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population, had channeled their “frustration and despair” into “hope.” He said he wanted to replace Mr. Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way” and that his first priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” that achieved that goal. The Arab parties’ strong showing may make them kingmakers. But building a governing coalition with Arab participation remains a fraught exercise in Israel. Many Israeli Jews believe that a parliamentary majority should not rely on the support of Arab lawmakers. People waiting to cast ballots in Umm al-Fahm, one of the largest Arab towns in Israel, on Tuesday. Credit... Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Most Arab citizens are the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homes during the 1948 Arab-Israel war at the time of Israel’s independence. Today, they mostly live in separate towns from Jewish Israelis and face violence and discriminatory housing policies. Over the decades, disagreements, including over Israel’s nature as a Jewish state, have led many Arab voters to avoid the ballot box. This week, many Arab voters said they were furious at Mr. Netanyahu for his treatment of the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and for policies that they feel treat Palestinians in Israel as second-class citizens. Indeed, throughout the campaign, Mr. Netanyahu made overt appeals to anti-Arab prejudice. “I’m very optimistic because people understand that this isn’t like ordinary elections — we want change,” said Kholoud Al-Zeinati, 39, an Arab Israeli voter who cast her ballot on Tuesday in the mixed Jewish-Arab city of Lod, where long lines formed at polling places. “Because we, as the Arab community, are the community that pays the biggest price across so many aspects of life, it’s important to come out and take part.” “I expect our votes to be truly decisive in shaping the next government and making things better for all of us,” she added. Of the two Arab parties that did well on Tuesday, only Raam has joined a coalition government in the past. That happened in 2021, when it joined the short-lived anti-Netanyahu coalition of Prime Minister Naftali Bennett. Raam’s participation in that government outraged many right-wing Jewish voters, and when it collapsed after roughly one year, they backed Mr. Netanyahu, who went on to form the most hard-line government in Israel’s history. That government now faces the possibility that it may be brought down by an election result that has been deeply shaped by robust Arab turnout. Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting from Lod, Israel. The longevity of his most recent governing coalition followed three years during which a cycle of collapsed coalitions and five snap elections had left the country without a functional government or national budget. In 2021, Israelis ousted Mr. Netanyahu from power and then returned him to office 18 months later. He had staged a previous comeback, in 2009, becoming prime minister a decade after his party was voted out of power. March 2021 Ousted by a single-seat majority In 2021, Mr. Netanyahu’s government collapsed after failing to pass a budget, setting off legislative elections. At the time, he had been indicted on charges of fraud, bribery and breach of trust , and the coalition he was leading was shaky. According to analysts , heading into an election was a gambit by Mr. Netanyahu to strengthen his grip on power before his criminal trial. But the electorate that voted that March didn’t give him the seats he needed, ending a period of 12 straight years in office for him. It took months of wrangling for an eclectic coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces to cobble together a single-seat majority in the Parliament. Naftali Bennett, a right-wing former ally of Mr. Netanyahu’s, led the coalition as prime minister, hammering out a deal with Yair Lapid, a centrist and former broadcaster who was appointed foreign minister. The eight-party coalition proved too unwieldy to endure. After two right-wing lawmakers defected and several on the left rebelled in critical votes, that government collapsed in June 2022 . November 2022 Returned to office by a hard-line coalition After the resulting elections, held in November 2022, Mr. Netanyahu returned to power as right-wing voters moved to more extreme parties, diminishing the center left. Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party allied with far-right and ultra-Orthodox lawmakers to secure a clear majority in the Parliament , forming the most hard-line and religious conservative government in Israel’s history. The coalition accounted for 48.4 percent of the vote but had a parliamentary majority because two anti-Netanyahu parties — one leftist, one Arab nationalist — fell just short of the share of votes needed to obtain seats. It was a reminder of how tiny swings among voters can have a big effect under Israel’s parliamentary system. Mr. Netanyahu has since overseen an acceleration of the country’s rightward shift, including an effort to overhaul the judiciary that prompted huge street protests. Questions about whether his government could have better pre-empted the Oct. 7 attack have also become hot-button issues . In April, Mr. Lapid and Mr. Bennett said they would reconstitute their centrist alliance of 2021 for the 2026 election. Mr. Netanyahu will also face Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who leads the largest opposition party . “It’s over,” he said. “It’s only a matter of time.” The comments were a reflection of Israel’s deepening global isolation, with even once-staunch allies imposing or threatening economic sanctions and embargoes after years of war in Gaza and rampant violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. With settlers advancing into areas that were previously off limits, Britain last month decried what it called “ethnic cleansing” and announced trade sanctions on settlements that it said would also apply to entities that financed their construction. Though Israel’s banking system has not been directly targeted by sanctions, a dozen countries, including Canada, France and Spain, have said they support restrictions on trade with settlements, raising the prospect of further penalties that could affect Israeli financial institutions. items.title: Live Updates: At Least 64 Killed in Train Crash in Spain, Officials Say
items.summary: A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another near Toledo, months after a crash involving the same carriers killed dozens and stunned the country.
items.full_text: Oct. 28, 2026, 10:01 a.m. ET José Bautista Reporting from the scene In the middle of fields of alfalfa and almond trees, a seemingly endless procession of ambulances, police cars and firetrucks drove in and out of the crash scene, as rescue helicopters flew low overhead. The trains seemed twisted together, a mass of mangled metal. Dozens of Civil Guard officers, some wearing the white protective suits used by forensic investigators, were inspecting the scene and gathering evidence. Broken cables and fallen utility poles were scattered all around. A group of Catholic priests walked out from the area where the trains were located. “We came to pray for the dead,” said the Rev. Luis Lucendo, 63, a vicar of Toledo and parish priest in Villacañas, a nearby town. “One man told us that his wife had died, and I was able to make the sign of the cross over her,” Father Lucendo said. “They were going to spend the day in Córdoba, but this is where their journey ended.” Credit... Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Oct. 28, 2026, 9:37 a.m. ET At least 64 people were killed in the train crash, the emergency services of Castilla-La Mancha said on Wednesday afternoon. The toll makes the accident one of the deadliest in the country’s history. Oct. 28, 2026, 9:26 a.m. ET Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez is traveling to Urda to offer support to first responders and express his support to the families of victims, his government said. Credit... Omar Havana/Associated Press Oct. 28, 2026, 8:39 a.m. ET Spain’s Civil Guard said on social media that it had set up offices in Madrid, Seville, Córdoba and Toledo for family members of potential victims. The primary goal is to identify missing persons through the collection of DNA samples, the agency said. Oct. 28, 2026, 8:35 a.m. ET The president of Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, confirmed that at least 30 people had been killed in the train crash, a number that may rise. About 80 people were injured, 50 of them, according to Mr. García-Page, with severe injuries. Oct. 28, 2026, 7:53 a.m. ET Blood donation groups in the area of the train crash are urging donors to come to hospitals in Toledo and Ciudad Real to “urgently replenish the reserves. Blood of all types will be needed.” Oct. 28, 2026, 7:32 a.m. ET Videos shot by passengers after the crash show parts of the derailed carriages pulverized, with charred wheels, and bags and seats strewn across an embankment. Emergency workers tend to the injured or hover over people covered in Mylar blankets. The arid field outside the small towns of Los Yébenes and Urda has become a parking lot of emergency vehicles and tents. Credit... Manu Fernandez/Associated Press Oct. 28, 2026, 7:24 a.m. ET Video filmed inside one of the trains and verified by The New York Times shows smoke rising from a charred, mangled carriage on the slope of the rail line. The footage was first shared by the Spanish radio station Capital Radio, which said an employee had been on one of the trains at the time of the crash. Video Credit Credit... Capital Radio, via Agence France-Presse Oct. 28, 2026, 6:37 a.m. ET The first eyewitness reports from the crash are beginning to trickle in on Spanish media. Passengers are describing an awful impact that tossed people from the dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. Passengers crawled out of windows and lay in in a nearby field, where local workers, who heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies. Credit... Javier Soriano/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Oct. 28, 2026, 6:27 a.m. ET The crash comes months after a deadly collision in January in southern Spain that involved the same carriers. That accident, in which two high-speed trains collided, killing 46 people, was the country’s worst railway disaster since 2013. An official report on what caused the January crash is not yet available, but preliminary investigations pointed to a broken rail as the likely cause. Oct. 28, 2026, 6:22 a.m. ET Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement that it was deploying a military emergency unit and Civil Guard officers to the scene of the crash in the province of Toledo. Investigators from Spain’s Major Disaster Unit are also en route.
